method.method_draft: Label the four vertices from the image as A = bottom-left, B = top apex, C = bottom/front, and D = right/back. Read the visible edge lengths as AB = 7, AC = 2, BD = 3, and CD = 4. The two unlabeled edges are BC, the central front edge, and AD, the dashed hidden edge. From the text, all side lengths are integers. Apply the strict triangle inequality to each triangular face. For BC: face ABC gives |7 - 2| < BC < 7 + 2, so 5 < BC < 9; face BCD gives |4 - 3| < BC < 4 + 3, so 1 < BC < 7. The only integer satisfying both is BC = 6. For AD: face ABD gives |7 - 3| < AD < 7 + 3, so 4 < AD < 10; face ACD gives |4 - 2| < AD < 4 + 2, so 2 < AD < 6. The only integer satisfying both is AD = 5. Add the two missing lengths: 6 + 5 = 11.

method.method_draft: Read the diagram as a tetrahedron with known edges 7 and 2 meeting at the left-bottom/top/front face, and known edges 3 and 4 meeting at the right/back face. Let x be the unlabeled central edge joining the endpoints of the 7-and-2 pair and also the endpoints of the 3-and-4 pair. Instead of listing all face candidates, bound x directly: it must be longer than the larger necessary difference, max(7 - 2, 4 - 3) = 5, and shorter than the smaller possible two-edge path, min(7 + 2, 3 + 4) = 7. Since x is an integer, x = 6. Let y be the dashed hidden edge. It is paired with known edges 7 and 3 in one adjacent face, and with known edges 2 and 4 in the other adjacent face. Thus y must satisfy max(7 - 3, 4 - 2) < y < min(7 + 3, 4 + 2), i.e. 4 < y < 6. Since y is an integer, y = 5. Therefore the required sum is 6 + 5 = 11.
